#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)

## ARIMA vs. ETS

```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Figure 1: Monthly U.S. sales at beer, wine, and liquor stores."
liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "U.S. Retail Sales at Beer, Wine, and Liquor Stores",
       x = "Month", y = "Millions of dollars (NSA)")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Figure 2: Season plot of log sales, one line per year."
liquor |>
  mutate(log_sales = log(sales)) |>
  gg_season(log_sales) +
  labs(title = "Season Plot of log(Liquor Store Sales)",
       x = "Month", y = "log(sales)")
```

Sales trend steadily upward over the whole sample. The seasonal pattern is strong and regular. December is by far the highest month because of the holidays, there's a smaller bump from May through August, and January and February are the lowest months. In Figure 1 the seasonal swings get bigger as sales grow, so the seasonality is multiplicative. Taking logs makes the swings about the same size every year, which is why we model log(sales).

```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

fable chose an ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1)\[12\] with drift and an ETS(A,A,A).

The ARIMA has d = 0 and D = 1, so log sales were not differenced month to month, but they were seasonally differenced once. That means the model works with the change in log sales from the same month a year earlier.

For the ETS, the first A means the errors are additive, the second A means the trend is additive (linear), and the third A means the seasonality is additive. Since the model is fit to log sales, additive seasonality in logs is the same as multiplicative seasonality in dollars.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Figure 3: Residual test and Ljung Box for the ARIMA model."
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
```

The model has p + q + P + Q = 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 6 estimated AR and MA coefficients, so dof = 6. The Ljung–Box statistic is about 120 with a p-value of essentially zero, so the residuals do not look like white noise. Several spikes in the ACF fall outside the blue bands, with the biggest one at lag 23.

With 336 months in the sample and a first training sample of 120 months, the TS-CV uses 216 forecast origins. The first forecast is for January 2002 and the last is for December 2019.

```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "One-month-ahead forecast accuracy, January 2002 to December 2019.")
```

ARIMA forecasts most accurately. It has the lowest RMSE and the lowest MAE, so the two metrics agree.

```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)
```

ARIMA vs. ETS has a DM statistic of -2.91 with a p-value of 0.004, and ARIMA vs. the seasonal random walk has a DM statistic of -10.76 with a p-value below 2.2e-16. Both statistics are negative, so ARIMA had the smaller squared errors each time, and both p-values are below 0.05, so ARIMA is significantly more accurate than both. If I were the liquor store chain, I would use the ARIMA model.

## Forecast Combination

```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Forecast accuracy including the equal-weight ARIMA/ETS combination.")
```

The combination has an RMSE of 85.19 and an MAE of 66.77. That is better than ETS but worse than ARIMA, so it lands in between the two models that go into it.

```{r}
#| echo: false
cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
```

The ARIMA and ETS forecast errors have a correlation of 0.88, so the two models mostly make the same mistakes and averaging them cancels out very little error. The DM test also showed ARIMA is significantly more accurate than ETS, so averaging in ETS just pulled the forecast toward the worse model. That is why the combination couldn't beat ARIMA.

## VAR vs. BVAR

```{r}
#| echo: false
qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))

growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]

var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

fc_bvar_03 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")
```

We produce 120 forecasts for each variable. The first is for 1990 Q1 and the last is for 2019 Q4.

```{r}
#| echo: false
var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")

var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "RMSE of one-quarter-ahead forecasts, 1990 Q1 to 2019 Q4.")
```

The VAR(1) forecasts better than the VAR(4) for 7 of the 8 variables, and inflation is basically a tie. Even though the VAR(4) contains the VAR(1) as a special case, it has 264 coefficients instead of 72, and each one is estimated with some error. That extra estimation noise ends up in the forecasts (overfitting), so the smaller model does better.

The BVAR(4) with λ = 0.3 beats the OLS VAR(4) for all 8 variables. They have the same variables and the same lags, so the difference comes from the Minnesota prior shrinking the coefficients toward zero, which cuts down on the estimation noise.

Compared to the VAR(1), the results are mixed. The BVAR is better for investment, inflation, and the 10-year yield, and the VAR(1) is better for the other five, but most of the differences are small.

With λ = 0.05, the forecasts get worse for 7 of the 8 variables, especially employment and inflation. Only the federal funds rate improves. This tells me λ = 0.05 is too much shrinkage, since it pushes the coefficients so close to zero that the model loses real dynamics in the data.

The winner's RMSE here would not be a fair estimate of how it will forecast in the future. I would be choosing the model based on these same 120 quarters, so some of its edge is luck, and its RMSE would look better than it will actually do going forward. A fair estimate would need data that wasn't used to pick the model.

```{r}
#| echo: false
e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

e_var4 <- actual[, "infl"] - fc_var4[, 5]
e_bvar <- actual[, "infl"] - fc_bvar_03[, 5]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)
```

For GDP growth, DM = 2.14 with a p-value of 0.035, so the BVAR is significantly more accurate at the 5% level. For inflation, DM = 1.45 with a p-value of 0.149, so the BVAR does better but the difference isn't significant. This makes me more careful about the table in 4.3b, since some of the gaps between models could just be noise.

## Factor Model

```{r}
#| echo: false
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,                      # level
         "2" = d(x),                   # first difference
         "3" = d(d(x)),                # second difference
         "4" = log(x),                 # log
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),        # growth rate
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),     # change in the growth rate
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)

tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
```

INDPRO and PAYEMS both use code 5, which is the monthly growth rate. CPIAUCSL uses code 6, which is the change in the monthly inflation rate. FEDFUNDS uses code 2, which is the first difference, so the monthly change in percentage points.

Industrial production is an index that grows exponentially over time, so the log growth rate makes it stationary. The federal funds rate is already a percent and sat near zero from about 2009 to 2015, where taking logs would blow up, so the change in percentage points makes more sense.

```{r}
#| echo: false
Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))

summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]
```

The first three factors explain 29.5% of the variation in all 121 series, which matches what we saw in class.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Figure 4: The first factor estimated from FRED-MD, signed to rise with industrial production."
F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))

tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```

The first factor is most correlated with employment (PAYEMS, USGOOD, MANEMP, DMANEMP), industrial production (INDPRO, IPMANSICS, IPFPNSS), and manufacturing capacity utilization (CUMFNS), so it captures real activity, or the business cycle. In the plot it drops sharply in big recessions like the early 1980s and 2008–09.

The second factor is most correlated with CPI and PCE price indexes (CPIAUCSL, CPITRNSL, CPIULFSL, PCEPI, and others), so it captures prices, or inflation.

```{r}
#| echo: false
ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
```

I get an RMSE of 0.617 for the AR(1) and 0.589 with the factors, which matches the numbers from class. Estimating the factors once on the full sample would be cheating, because at a forecast origin like 1995 the factors would be using data through 2019 that nobody had yet. That would make the factor model look better than it could actually do in real time.

```{r}
#| echo: false
direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                      # growth over the latest month

  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                     varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4, caption = "Direct 12-month-ahead forecasts of CPI inflation, with and without factors.")
```

Yes, the factors improve the forecast of 12-month CPI inflation. The RMSE drops from 2.108 to 1.894, about a 10.2% reduction, and the DM p-value is 0.0004, so the difference is statistically significant.

## Reflection

The biggest thing I took away from this problem set is that simple models are hard to beat, especially when there isn't much data compared to the number of parameters. The VAR(1) beat the VAR(4), and a lot of the differences between models weren't statistically significant once I actually tested them. The same idea kept coming up in different forms, which was giving up a little bias to cut down on estimation noise. Shrinkage in the BVAR, equal weights in the combination, and factors that squeeze 121 series down to three all let a model use a lot of information without estimating a lot of parameters. I also learned that how the test is set up matters, like re-estimating the factors at every forecast origin instead of using the full sample. I feel like I have a better understanding of the forecasting process in general now. As before, AI disclosure as AI was used to help fix broken code. I went back and reviewed its corrections and spent time understanding why my code didn't and why the generative code was successful. AI was sparsely used for the write up, mainly to fix clunky hard to understand wording. All was reviewed by me, and edited as needed.
